lead: One shared store holds every value that many parts of the screen need. Only a plain function called a reducer may replace that state, and only in response to a plain object called an action. So every change has a name, a recorded before and after, and a reason. Redux, built on the earlier Flux architecture, is used in React carts, dashboards and admin panels where a bug report says "the count is wrong after I press back". This chapter builds a cart reducer and traces three dispatches through it.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for props, state and lifting state up, and 5.3 for the event handlers that dispatch actions.

sections.h3: Why shared state needs one home

blocks.text: In 5.2 state lived inside one component. That works until two far-apart components need the same value: a header shows a cart badge, a product list adds items, a checkout page reads the total. Lift the state to a common parent and every component in between receives props it never uses. That is prop drilling. Three symptoms follow: long prop chains, sibling components drifting out of sync, and bugs that are hard to reproduce because many setState calls spread the truth across the tree.

Flux is the architecture Facebook described for React. Data moves one way only. A view creates an action, a dispatcher sends it to the stores, the stores update, and the views re-render from the stores. Nothing writes back into a view or into another store.

Redux is Flux with two simplifications. One store for the whole app instead of several. And no dispatcher: the store hands each action straight to a pure function called the reducer. Fewer moving parts, the same one-way loop.

The store is one object that holds the whole state tree. It has three methods: getState() returns the current state, dispatch(action) sends an action in, and subscribe(listener) registers a function the store calls after every change.

An action is a plain object: {type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: {id: 1, name: 'Masala dosa', price: 60}}. type is a required string, payload carries the data, and Redux throws an error when type is undefined. An action creator is a small function that returns this object, so the string 'ADD_ITEM' is typed in one place only.

A reducer is a pure function (state = initialState, action) => newState. Pure means the same inputs give the same output, with no mutation of the argument, no fetch, no Date.now() and no Math.random(). It switches on action.type, and the default branch returns state unchanged, so unknown actions cost nothing. combineReducers({cart: cartReducer, user: userReducer}) joins small reducers into the shape {cart: ..., user: ...}.

blocks.where: reducer is the pure function; currentState is the object inside the store before the dispatch; action is {type, payload}; nextState is a new object and the store replaces currentState with it.

items: A component calls dispatch({type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: item}).
The store passes the current state and the action to the reducer.
The reducer matches the type and returns a new object, leaving the old one untouched.
The store saves the new object and calls every subscribed listener, so React re-renders the components whose selected slice changed.

sections.h3: React-Redux, immutability and the lighter option

blocks.text: React-Redux joins the store to React. Wrap the app once in the Provider component from react-redux, with the prop store={store}, where store is the object returned by createStore or configureStore. Every component below it can then read a slice with const count = useSelector(state => state.cart.count) and send actions with const dispatch = useDispatch(). Older code uses connect() with mapStateToProps and mapDispatchToProps; the idea is the same.

Never edit state in place. push and state.count++ change the existing object, and Redux compares old and new by reference: the same reference means "nothing changed", so no re-render. Copy first, then change.

Async work: redux-thunk is one middleware that lets an action creator return a function instead of an object, so it can fetch and then dispatch the real action. Redux Toolkit's createSlice writes action types and reducers together and copies state for you. Middleware sits between dispatch and the reducer: redux-thunk for async work, redux-logger for logging. The Redux DevTools time-travel slider comes from a store enhancer, applied through the devTools option of configureStore or composeWithDevTools, not from middleware.

The Context API is React's built-in version: createContext, a Provider, and useContext, with no library. It suits a theme, a language or the logged-in user. It has no action log and no time travel. Redux is overkill when one value is shared, or when the state belongs to a single form — keep that in useState.

spec.aria: Four state cards stacked top to bottom, joined by three actions: add dosa 60, add coffee 40, remove id 1; the totals go 0, 60, 100, 40 and the count 0, 1, 2, 1.

examples.question: A cart reducer starts from {items: [], count: 0, total: 0}. ADD_ITEM appends payload to items, adds 1 to count and payload.price to total. REMOVE_ITEM drops the item whose id equals payload.id, subtracts 1 from count and payload.price from total. The app dispatches in order: (1) ADD_ITEM {id: 1, name: 'Masala dosa', price: 60}; (2) ADD_ITEM {id: 2, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 40}; (3) REMOVE_ITEM {id: 1, price: 60}. Trace the state after each dispatch and give the final items, count and total.
steps: Before any dispatch: items = [], count = 0, total = 0 rupees.
Dispatch 1, ADD_ITEM dosa at 60 rupees: items = [...[], dosa] = 1 item; count = 0 + 1 = 1; total = 0 + 60 = 60 rupees. The initial object is not edited.
Dispatch 2, ADD_ITEM coffee at 40 rupees: items = [dosa, coffee] = 2 items; count = 1 + 1 = 2; total = 60 + 40 = 100 rupees.
Dispatch 3, REMOVE_ITEM id 1 at 60 rupees: items = the 2 items filtered to id not equal to 1 = [coffee] = 1 item; count = 2 − 1 = 1; total = 100 − 60 = 40 rupees.
Final state: {items: [{id: 2, name: 'Filter coffee', price: 40}], count: 1, total: 40 rupees}.
The badge shows 1 and the total shows 40 rupees, because the store handed React a new object at every step.
examples.answer: After three dispatches the cart holds one item, Filter coffee at 40 rupees, with count = 1 and total = 40 rupees.

traps: A reducer that does state.items.push(item) or state.count = state.count + 1 returns the same object reference. React-Redux sees no change and the badge stays stale.
An action must be a plain object with a string type. dispatch({payload: x}) throws 'Actions may not have an undefined type property'.
Reducers must stay pure. An API call, Date.now() or Math.random() inside gives different states for the same action, so tests and DevTools time travel lie.
count is not items.length once you allow the same product twice with a quantity. Fix the rule in the question before you trace it.
Dispatching during render, instead of inside an event handler, re-renders, dispatches again, and loops forever.

quiz.q: Which properties does a Redux action carry, and which one is required?
quiz.a: type, a required string, and payload, the optional data.

quiz.q: Name the three methods of a Redux store.
Why must a reducer be pure?
quiz.a: So the same action on the same state always gives the same new state. That makes tests, logging and DevTools time travel correct.

quiz.q: How did Redux simplify the Flux architecture?
quiz.a: One store instead of many, and no dispatcher: the store calls a reducer directly with the action.

quiz.q: The cart state is {count: 2, total: 100}. An ADD_ITEM action with price 25 is dispatched. Give the new count and total.
A component still shows the old count after a dispatch. Give two possible causes.
quiz.a: Two real causes: (1) the reducer mutated state and returned the same object reference, so React-Redux saw no change; (2) the component copied the value once into local useState, or reads a different slice or a different store instance, instead of reading it from useSelector on each render, so it never re-reads the updated value.

quiz.q: When would you choose the Context API over Redux?
quiz.a: Few shared values that change rarely, such as theme, language or logged-in user, in a small app that needs no middleware, action log or time travel.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hand-written switch reducers are now rare: Redux Toolkit's createSlice and RTK Query, which caches server data, are the default, while Zustand, Jotai and Recoil offer smaller hook-based stores. React Server Components move some data fetching off the client. XState models state as an explicit machine instead of a bag of fields. Search 'Redux Toolkit createSlice', 'RTK Query' and 'Zustand vs Redux' next.
